title: AND, OR & NOT
goal: Make an IF check two conditions at once: both must be true (AND), at least one must be true (OR), or the opposite must be true (NOT), and tell which one a real rule needs.

steps.text:
A scholarship needs **marks of at least 60 and attendance of at least 75**. One IF can only ask one question, so how do you ask two?

You put **AND** inside the IF: `=IF(AND(B2>=60,C2>=75),"Yes","No")`. AND says “yes” only when **every** test inside it is true.

Farah has good marks but poor attendance. Click the button and watch ==D3==.

steps.prompt:
For Ben, two cells decide the answer: his marks **and** his attendance.

Select both: press on ==B3==, drag across to ==C3==, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: Ben is on row 3. Start on his marks (`B3`) and drag one cell right to his attendance (`C3`).
clues: The Name Box should read `1R x 2C` when you have it right.

steps.prompt:
Click ==D3== and type `=IF(AND(B3>=60,C3>=75),"Yes","No")`, then press [[Enter]].

The two tests sit inside **AND**, separated by a comma. The IF still has its usual three parts.
steps.explain: Ben's marks pass (80) but his attendance doesn't (60 is below 75). AND needs **both**, so one failed test is enough to give **No**.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use both `IF` and `AND`: the AND goes inside the IF's first slot.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets: `AND(` closes after both tests, then the IF carries on with its two answers.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Ben's attendance is only 60, below the 75 needed. Check both tests are inside `AND(...)` and `Yes` comes first.

clues: `AND(test1,test2)` goes where the single test used to be.

steps.prompt:
Tests inside AND can mix numbers and words.

A shop gives **free delivery** when the order is **500 or more** and the area is **Local**. In ==D3==, show **Free** or **Charge** for order 102.
steps.explain: Order 102 is **exactly** 500, and “500 or more” includes it, and the area is Local. Both tests pass, so **Free**. With `>` instead of `>=` it would wrongly say Charge.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets, and put quotes around each word: `"Local"`, `"Free"`, `"Charge"`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Order 102 is exactly 500 and Local, so both tests pass. Use `>=` for “500 or more”.

steps.prompt:
**OR** is the opposite mood: it says yes when **at least one** test is true.

A cinema gives a discount to anyone aged **60 or more**, or with a **student card**. Click ==D3== and type `=IF(OR(B3>=60,C3="Yes"),"Discount","Full price")`.
steps.explain: Sneha has no student card, but at 67 she passes the age test, and one is enough for OR: **Discount**. AND would have said Full price here.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and the quote marks around words.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Sneha is 67, so the age test is true, and with OR one true test is enough. Did you use `OR(` and not `AND(`?

clues: `OR(B3>=60,C3="Yes")` is true if either test is true.

steps.prompt:
A shop reviews a product when its **rating is below 3** or it has **2 or more complaints**.

In ==D3==, show **Review** or **OK** for the Toaster.
steps.explain: The Toaster's rating of 3 is **not** below 3, but its 2 complaints meet “2 or more”. One true test is enough, so **Review**.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and the quote marks.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Test each one for the Toaster: is 3 below 3? And are 2 complaints “2 or more”? Remember `<` for below and `>=` for “or more”.

steps.prompt:
**NOT** flips a test: it turns yes into no, and no into yes. It's handy for saying “everything except…”.

Chase every invoice that is **not Paid**. In ==C3==, show **Chase** or **Fine** for invoice 202. Use `NOT(B3="Paid")` as your test.
steps.explain: `B3="Paid"` is false for an Overdue invoice, and NOT flips that to true, so the answer is **Chase**. You'll meet NOT most often wrapped around an AND or OR.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Use `IF` and put `NOT(...)` around the test.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets: `NOT(B3="Paid")` is the test, inside the IF.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Invoice 202 is Overdue, so it must be chased. Chase goes in the **yes** slot, because `NOT(B3="Paid")` is true for it.

clues: `=IF(NOT(B3="Paid"),` then the yes-answer, then the no-answer.

steps.prompt:
Back to the scholarship. Ben has **80 marks** but **60 attendance**, so `D3` says **No** under AND.

The college relaxes the rule: **either** 60+ marks **or** 75+ attendance. Before you change anything, what will `D3` show with OR?
options: An error, as you can't swap AND for OR
steps.explain: OR only needs **one** true test, and Ben's 80 marks are above 60. So the same data gives **Yes** under OR and **No** under AND. Swapping the word changes the rule.
wrongFeedback: That would be right for AND. With OR, one passing test is enough, and Ben's marks pass.
Both are ordinary functions that take the same tests. You can swap one for the other freely.
clues: Which of Ben's two tests is true?

steps.prompt: Time to check. `D3` has the AND formula. Replace it with the OR version, so the **same Ben** is eligible if marks are 60+ **or** attendance is 75+.
steps.explain: Same data, same tests, one word changed, and the answer flipped from No to **Yes**. Always ask yourself “must both be true, or is one enough?” before choosing AND or OR.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: Swap `AND` for `OR` and keep the rest.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets: the two tests sit inside `OR(...)`.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Ben's marks are 80, which is at least 60. With `OR` that alone gives **Yes**. Is `AND` still in your formula?

steps.prompt:
Merit is for marks **from 60 to 90**. Someone used this formula, and now both **95** and **40** show Merit.

Why?
options: Every mark passes at least one test, so OR is always true
steps.explain: 95 is at least 60, so the first test passes. 40 is at most 90, so the second test passes. “Between” needs **both** limits to hold, so it's an **AND**, not an OR.
wrongFeedback: The `<=90` is the right way to say “at most 90”. The problem is how the two tests are joined.
IF can use as many tests as you like inside an AND or an OR.
clues: Does 95 pass the first test? Does 40 pass the second?

steps.prompt:
A running club puts anyone who finishes in **30 to 45 minutes** (both ends included) in the **Club** group. Everyone else goes in the **Open** group.

Put a formula in `C3` that shows Hari's group.
steps.explain: **Open.** Hari's 52 passes the “at least 30” test but fails “at most 45”. “Between two limits” needs both to hold, so you use AND.

wrongFeedback.missingFunction: This rule needs two tests that must **both** hold.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Make the formula look at Hari's time in `B3`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and the quote marks.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Hari took 52 minutes: too slow for the 30-to-45 group. If you got **Club**, check you joined the tests with AND, not OR.

clues: Two tests on the same cell: at least 30, and at most 45.
